summary: Explores issues with internationalized domain names that result from using different encodings, such as UTF-8 and Punycode. It stresses the importance of agreeing on a single encoding and how complicated things are with several in use.

eli5.summary: Domain names with fancy letters can be written in several ways. When programs disagree on the way, things break. This explains why picking one way matters.

questions: what is an a-label in idn
why do internationalized domain names fail to resolve
can dns names contain non-ascii characters
subtitle: Why domain names with non-ASCII characters break when applications and resolvers disagree on how to encode them.

tldr.problem: Internationalized domain names can be written as UTF-8 or as Punycode A-labels, and different protocols, APIs and private networks use different forms, so the same name can resolve in one place and fail in another.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB explains where the encodings collide (generic name resolution APIs, non-DNS protocols, private UTF-8 namespaces, suffix search lists) and recommends that only the component that knows which protocol is in use converts a name to its encoding.
tldr.outcome: General applications should not convert names to A-labels before calling protocol-independent resolver APIs, and resolvers should accept both forms. Doing it wrong can fail lookups or let an attacker claim the other encoding of a name.

today: RFC 6055 is an Informational IAB document published in February 2011. It updates RFC 2130 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC, according to the metadata for this entry.

sections.title: Encodings Behind Internationalized Names
sections.content:
An Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) is a domain name with at least one label containing non-ASCII characters. Like any name, each label has to be encoded before it goes into packets or onto disk. Unicode gives every character an integer code point (0 to 1,114,111), and UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32 are different ways to store those integers.

IDNA, the standard for IDNs on the public Internet, allows two forms of a valid label. A U-label is the Unicode characters directly. An A-label is an ASCII-compatible form produced by the Punycode algorithm and prefixed with xn--. The two forms are duals: converting between them loses no information.

The document also notes that comparing Unicode strings byte by byte is not enough, because there are many ways to represent the same characters. It only works when both strings are mapped to a canonical form and encoded the same way.
sections.eli5: A word with fancy letters can be stored as the fancy letters themselves, or as a plain-letters code that starts with xn--. Both mean the same thing, but a computer has to know which one it is looking at.

sections.title: The Real Name Resolution Architecture
sections.content:
The original IDNA specification described IDNA as a shim between an application and the DNS resolver library. The RFC calls that a simplistic picture, and gives two reasons it does not match reality.

  • Operating system resolver APIs such as getaddrinfo() are not DNS-specific. They may use DNS, mDNS, LLMNR, NetBIOS-over-TCP, a hosts table or NIS, and the application does not know which.
  • Even within DNS, private namespaces do not necessarily use the same character encoding as the public namespace.

Resolver APIs such as getaddrinfo() and gethostbyname() take C char * strings ended by a NULL byte. That works for ASCII, A-labels, ISO-2022-JP and UTF-8, but not for UTF-16 or UTF-32, where a zero byte can appear mid-string. Windows offers a separate API, GetAddrInfoW(), that takes UTF-16. The RFC says it is cleaner for an API to state its encoding explicitly than for callers to guess it.
sections.eli5: The program asking for a name does not know which phone book will be used to look it up. Each phone book may be written in a different code.

sections.title: Non-DNS Protocols and Non-ASCII in DNS
sections.content:
Some protocols use other forms than A-labels. Multicast DNS specifies UTF-8, and the IETF policy on character sets (RFC 2277) says protocols MUST be able to use UTF-8. If an application converts a name to an A-label and the resolver then falls back to such a protocol, the name is not found.

A common belief is that DNS only allows letters, digits and hyphens. The RFC traces this to the 1985 hosts-table definition and the 1987 RFC 1034 preferred name syntax. RFC 2181 clarified that the DNS itself restricts only length (labels of 1 to 63 octets, full names of 255 octets); any binary string can be a label. So UTF-8 names are legal in DNS.

UTF-8 also fits better than UTF-16 or UTF-32 because any 7-bit ASCII string is already valid UTF-8 and the encoding is byte-oriented, so endianness does not matter. Enterprises had put UTF-8 names in their private DNS namespaces, and the Punycode and xn-- prefix approach was developed later for the public namespace, so two encodings now coexist.
sections.eli5: People thought the phone book only allowed plain letters, but it never really did. Companies already wrote fancy-letter names in their own phone books before the code with xn-- was invented.

sections.title: What Goes Wrong in Practice
sections.content:
The RFC walks through cases that happen in existing implementations. In one, the user types a non-ASCII name and the application first converts it to an A-label such as xn--e1afmkfd.xn--80akhbyknj4f.com. DNS does not find it, the name resolution API tries mDNS, and mDNS fails because names there are registered in UTF-8.

In another, an application sends an A-label for a single label, the resolver appends a suffix from the search list, and the private namespace uses UTF-8, so every query fails. A third mixes a public IDNA zone with a private UTF-8 sub-zone, and the lookup fails because no server is found for the UTF-8 form of the parent.

Users also see inconsistent behavior across applications. Two competing browsers may differ in whether a name resolves, which can push users to switch applications. An application launched from another (a browser starting a media player) may resolve the same name differently.

If an attacker registers the same name in the other encoding, the user may reach the attacker's machine. The RFC compares this to phishing, except that both names represent exactly the same Unicode characters.
sections.eli5: If one helper uses the code and another does not, the same address works for one and fails for the other. A sneaky person could even set up a fake house at the address written in the other code.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
It is inappropriate for an application that calls a general-purpose name resolution library to convert a name to an A-label, unless it is absolutely certain that only the global DNS using A-labels will resolve the name in every environment where it might run. Conversion should be done by an entity that knows which protocol and which part of the namespace is in use, such as the DNS resolver or getaddrinfo() once it has chosen DNS.

A more intelligent resolver should be liberal in what it accepts: it may query for both the A-label form (over the Internet) and the UTF-8 form (over a corporate network with a private namespace). A stub resolver should accept either UTF-8 or A-labels in response data such as PTR records and convert to whatever the application API uses. APIs should state which encodings they accept; GetAddrInfoW() accepts only UTF-16, whereas the original getaddrinfo() specification does not say.

For DNS servers, storing separate records per encoding is undesirable because they could become inconsistent. A new server for a UTF-8 private namespace could treat encoding conversion like case-insensitive comparison, since conversion between A-labels and U-labels is unambiguous.
sections.eli5: Let the part of the system that knows which phone book is being used pick the right code. Apps should just hand over the name as it is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Having applications convert names to A-labels before calling name resolution can create vulnerabilities. If the name is resolved by protocols or in zones where records are registered in another encoding, an attacker can claim the A-label version of the same name and trick the victim into reaching a different destination. This applies to any non-ASCII name, with no case or language confusion needed.

The RFC points to RFC 4690 for other kinds of confusion. It also advises designers and users of ASCII-based encodings of Unicode to consider trademark protection and phishing, for example when an encoded name would naturally be associated with another organization or product.
sections.eli5: If two spellings of the same name lead to different places, a trickster can grab the one you did not expect.

data.title: Telling label encodings apart
data.code:
if label contains ESC (0x1B)      -> ISO-2022-JP
else if any byte has the high bit -> UTF-8
else if label starts with xn--    -> A-label
else                              -> ASCII (also UTF-8)
